utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning to those in court and those in Belgrade. And good morning to you, sir, the witness for today in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please stand and read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Now, we will commence this morning by asking Mr. Popovic if he has some questions for you, and you will, I expect, hear questions from him and you will answer him as though you were here in the courtroom because we can see and hear you, and you will be able to see and hear Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Spasic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, before we begin with our interview today, I will ask you. Because you and I speak the same language, after you hear the question please wait for a while and only then give your answer because in that way we shall enable the interpreters to do their work properly. Mr. Spasic, can you first of all please tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: My name is Slobodan Spasic, father's name Pavle.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 21st of April, 1946, in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what education do you have?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I'm a mechanical engineer. I have a BA in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, were you a member of the Ministry of the Interior; and if so, since when?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Ministry of the Interior since 1973 and until 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you retired in 2001?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I retired in late September 2001, at my own request.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, can you briefly explain for us what duties you were assigned to discharge within the Ministry of the Interior during your professional career.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of January, 1973, until November 1977, I worked in the republican secretariat of the interior, which is now the MUP, as an inspector for prevention and technical and fire prevention department. In late 1977, I was transferred to the secretariat of the interior in Belgrade as the commander of the firefighters' brigade in the city of Belgrade. I held this position for 12 years, after which I was appointed deputy chief of the administration for the fire prevention department of the secretariat in Belgrade. And after that, I was appointed chief of the administration for the fire prevention and technical department. And I held this position until 1994. After that, I was transferred to the Ministry of the Interior as the chief of the fire prevention police administration, and I remained in that position to the end of my career, that is to say until the time when I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please be more precise about the duties that you had in the Ministry of the Interior during 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: During 1998/1999, I was the chief of the administration of the fire police of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Spasic, before we deal with your scope of work, I wanted to ask you some basic things about the Ministry of the Interior. First of all, who is managing the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior is managed by the minister who is appointed by the government, with the approval of the Republic of Serbia, that is to say the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What authorities did the minister of the interior have in terms of discharging his duty?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The minister managed the work of the minister, he issued orders, instructions, regulations, and all the other authorities that he had according to the law; that was why he also had a team of associates who help him to discharge all these duties. He also had the authority as minister to make appointments or to dismiss people. He had quite extensive authorities in terms of the work of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me how were the duties discharged within the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say which organisational units did the ministry consist of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior had two basic organisational units to -- two departments. One was the state security department and the other one was the public security department. So these were the basic units that the ministry consisted of.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: As for the public security department, what were the organisational units that it consisted of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The public security department included organisational units which were active at the ministry seat, as we called it. These were various administrations, and we had the organisational units that were outside of the seat of the ministry and were still part of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, were there any territorial organisational units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. These were the secretariats of the interior, which were 33 in number in the territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Spasic. As for the subject that we're discussing now, I will ask for the document D357 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: P357.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be document under tab 1. If we could please pull that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: If you can see the document, these are the rules about the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior. Let us just go through it briefly in connection with the subject we're talking about. If we could look at Article 13 of these rules, it is page 9 in the B/C/S version and page 10 -- I apologise, page 9 in English version and page 10 in the B/C/S version of this document. Under Roman numeral III, the organisational units of the ministry, at the seat of the ministry, and their remit of work are mentioned. I have to say that I cannot see the document in front of me, and I hope that the Trial Chamber and other participants can see what I'm talking about. No? It's all right now. Please, Mr. Spasic, please have a look at Article 13 and give us a brief comment in connection with the subject that we were just talking about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: These are the organisational units which were active at the seat of the ministry. These are administrations which had certain authority to carry out certain duties. That was the crime police administration, the police administration, the traffic police administration, the operations centre, the border police administration for foreigners and administrative affairs, fire prevention, police administration, analysis administration, information technology administration, communications administration, administration for joint affairs of the ministry, and the board and lodging administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, can you tell us if the administration whose head you were in 1998/1999 is listed here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is under number 6, the fire prevention police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you mention that, can you please -- can we please have a look at Article 19, which is page 17 in B/C/S and page 15 in the English version. This is Article 19, the subtitle is the fire prevention police administration. Does this article regulate the duties which are part of the responsibility of the fire prevention police; and if so, can you tell us what were these duties and tasks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This article defines the duties and the authorities of the administration. The administration had the basic task to improve fire prevention. And in the prevention, it dealt with the problems of prevention work and the problems that fire-fighting units faced in their work. The basic task of this administration was to improve fire prevention by passing various rules, issuing instructions, co-ordinating the work in the field, monitoring special productions such as the production of gases, explosives. Then to issue regulations about safe work in terms of fire prevention. So that was one of the aspects of the administration's work. The other aspect was the control and improvement of the work of fire-fighting units in the territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of this article we can see that the administration had some departments. Can you please tell us what this was. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: As I said, the administration dealt with two groups of work. There were also two departments entrusted with jobs of that nature. One department was the department for the promotion and monitoring of fire-fighting activities, and the other department was the one for the monitoring of the work of the fire-fighting units. These were the main two task divisions actually in the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misic -- I'm sorry, Mr. Spasic. Who was your immediate superior in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: During 1998 and 1999 my immediate superior was deputy -- assistant minister, Major-General Stojan Misic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can we look at P263, which relates to your answer given just now. This is in tab 2 in your binder. So, Mr. Spasic, this is dispatch 650 of the 4th of June, 1997, sent by Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. Can you briefly comment on this dispatch, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: This dispatch signed by the minister, Vlajko Stojiljkovic, we are being informed about some personnel decisions within the ministry, stating that the acting chief of the public security sector would be Lieutenant-General Vlastimir Djordjevic, the deputy -- assistant ministers Petar Zekovic and Obrad Stevanovic were being appointed to these jobs and the powers of certain assistant ministers were being defined in order to deal with certain fields of work. Major-General Rade Markovic is being appointed as the assistant minister in charge of crime police; General Misic is being appointed as assistant minister for the administrative affairs for foreigners, administrative and legal affairs, and as well as fire prevention and communication affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, on the basis of this dispatch everyone was informed about the people appointed to deal with fire-fighting duties directly. But could you please tell us, who did you receive your orders and instructions from in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to this dispatch I received my instructions from Major-General Stojan Misic; however, some instructions I also received directly from the minister. So I was in the position of having to carry out certain instructions that I had received directly from the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The instructions that you received directly from the minister, was General Misic consulted or informed about these instructions? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I don't think that he was informed about it. I think that this was done without his knowledge, in view of the fact that while executing those instructions many things were not known to him that directly had to do with the things that I was instructed to do by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And these instructions that you received from the minister, did they have to do with your professional duties and the professional tasks of your administration?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately in certain situations the minister issued instructions that delved into the professional matters. So we had a lot of problems that had to do with instructions that were not sufficiently professionally grounded in terms of executing these assignments because he considered himself to be a professional in all the fields relating to security, including this very narrow specialised professional type of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any reasons or any grounds based on which the minister would consider himself to be competent in your professional area which you consider to be highly specialised?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know the reason for that because when I started out in the MUP in 1973, Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic was the chief of the secretariat of internal affairs in Pozarevac, one of the organisational units of the MUP. And he was at the head of that secretariat. After that he was transferred -- he actually moved into political and economic affairs. And on the basis of that, he considered himself to be competent and a professional in all aspects of MUP work because he had been a chief of a small secretariat and felt this was a qualification which would allow him to declare himself a professional in many spheres and to issue orders pertaining to those professional spheres.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, for the purposes of the transcript could you please repeat your answer about the specific areas the minister felt he was a professional in.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: For all areas that had to do with public security, including traffic police work, fire-fighting, administrative affairs. He considered himself to be an expert. Since he had once been a chief he felt that he was competent in all these areas and that he could provide a competent view relating to all areas of public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, you talked about your personal experience, but where is your information coming from about the experience of other administration chiefs and heads of other administrations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: This type of work that I had the opportunity to see, to experience, if I can put it that way, was something that other colleagues also had the opportunity to see, to see this attitude. This is something that we discussed amongst ourselves because often these would be orders that were actually not justified from a professional expert point of view. So this is something that we would discuss amongst ourselves, we would discuss these problems. But we were forced to carry out the minister's orders because he was our highest-ranking superior. I spoke with my colleagues who were working on the same floor that I was working on. These were my colleagues from the crime fighting police, such as Dragan Ilic, who would often during the week speak with me. We would spend time together, and then it would happen that during our conversation there would be a call from the minister or he would be receiving some orders from him over the telephone. So this manner of work was something that not only I was familiar with, but all the other superior officers were in the position to receive direct orders from the minister and to be also accountable to the minister for the implementation of those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Spasic, other than the topics that we spoke about, how did the minister handle or manage the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: There were different ways. There were documents, written documents, that were issued, but his main manner or method of work was through the collegium which would meet at regular intervals, for example, every Monday or every Tuesday they would meet regularly. So that was one of the ways of managing the ministry which was used not only by Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic, this was a method used by other ministers too. This was one of the ways of managing the ministry by using the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain the collegium as a management method of the MUP, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The collegium functioned in such a way that corresponded to what the minister wanted. When I came to the service in 1994, this was a public security service collegium, and it was headed by the chief of the public security administration. And all the chiefs of administrations would participate in the collegium meeting. With the arrival of Vlajko Stojiljkovic, the collegium -- he actually placed himself at the head of the collegium and a different method or relationship came into being. His method of work was different. Once he came, the collegium became the collegium of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about the collegium, I would like us to focus primarily on the period which began when Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic was appointed the minister of the interior, and I would like us to look at that period from the point of time when he came to the head of the ministry and then the period up to December 1998 and then the period after December 1998. And I'm going to show you a document which will indicate why I'm focusing on that period. But could you please explain how the collegium started to operate from the point in time when Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic became minister.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: When Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic assumed his duties, the collegium -- he personally would attend the collegium meetings, and it -- the sessions were opened as a rule by the chief of the public security department. Then he would give the floor to the minister, who would then give us a relatively brief report. He would give us an assessment of the security situation, and then he would receive reports from the chiefs of the administrations, which is what we would do. We would speak about the work of the administrations, the problems that had occurred between two collegium sessions. After that, reports would be submitted or would report on matters of interest, the assistant ministers. And then the minister would conclude the collegium session by issuing assignments for the forthcoming period, which we were expected to include in our plan of work and which we were supposed to implement. Minutes were kept and the collegium was attended by a member of the analysis administration. So after going through all the documents which would be something that he was in charge of, we would be given the minutes from that particular collegium session where the tasks issued by the minister for the forthcoming period would also be stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, can we go back to your previous answer because the transcript does not reflect what you answered to me. I'm going to put the question to you again. These are lines 8 and 9 on page 11. Can you please tell me what happened -- or rather, what happened to the collegium of the public security chief from the point in time when Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic assumed his duties as minister?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a major difference. Before he arrived, the collegiums were not attended by representatives of the state security department. With the arrival of Vlajko Stojiljkovic, members -- actually, the chief of the State Security Service and his deputy, Mr. Rade Markovic and Mr. Curcic also attended these collegium meetings. This was a change in the work of the collegium because the state security representatives, these two, would also attend this meeting of all the chiefs of the public security service departments, because this was not the case before. The work of the collegium did not include the attendance by these two representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: My question is the following. You did clarify that, but it's represented a little bit differently in the transcript. So can you please answer the following. Is it true that from the point in time Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic came to the ministry as minister, there was a collegium of the chiefs of the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did exist. The collegium existed. I don't know how to call it. It was the -- not in the same composition to include members of the State Security Service. We didn't call it the public security sector collegium anymore. It became the collegium of the minister. This is what we called it and it was attended by all the chiefs of the public security sector and representatives of the state security sector. From the point in time that Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic became minister, it was no longer the collegium of the public security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: From the point in time when Vlajko Stojiljkovic came to head the ministry, was there any other collegium in existence, other than the one that you have just described to us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I don't know of any other collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask to look at D208, please. Mr. Spasic, this is the decision on the forming of the collegium issued by the minister. The date is the 4th of December, 1998, and this is the reason why I in my previous questions asked you about the period up to the 4th of December, 1998, and now we're going to talk about the period after the 4th of December, 1998. First of all, can you tell us, looking at this decision, what the composition of the collegium was that was established by the minister.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: This decision names the members of the collegium, and this decision was adopted after Mr. Radomir Markovic was promoted to the post of chief of the public security department. And the decision refers to a certain number of public security and a certain number of state security officials as the collegium members. And we can see from the decision that there was no assistant minister for crime fighting. This was when Dragan Ilic was appointed as chief of the crime prevention and fighting administration. The chief of the secretariat in Belgrade also participated in the collegium. This ministerial collegium comprised representatives from the public security sector and representatives from the state security sector, with the proviso that it also included the assistant ministers, except for Dragan Ilic who did not have that rank but was in charge of crime-fighting affairs, because Rade Markovic who was assistant minister for crime fighting was not replaced by anyone who would then be in charge of that particular section.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Spasic. Just for the transcript, what was the function that Mr. Radomir Markovic had?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Do you mean before or after the 4th of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: After the 4th of December.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: He was the assistant minister, and he was chief of the state security department, Radomir Markovic I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I will ask you to have a look with me at page 2 of this document. And before I direct your attention to a specific paragraph of this document, please tell me: Did you attend the meetings of the collegium after the 4th of December, 1998?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I attended the meetings of the collegium because this decision made it possible to invite other people to the collegium meetings, if these people were invited by the minister. That was why I attended the meetings of the collegium and participated in its work. By this decision, it was envisaged that the minister could invite others who were not personally listed in the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Spasic. As you have given such answer, can we please now look at the last page of this document, that is page 4. We can see a paper that says collegium, list of collegium participants, and certain persons are listed here. Can you please have a look at the list of these persons and tell us whether these persons attended the meetings of the collegium. Is there anyone who is left out, or is there any person who is listed here but did not attend the meetings of the collegium?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, and as I'm looking at the list of the participants of the collegium now, Miodrag Zavisic, who is listed here, did not attend the meetings. As far as I remember, the others mostly did attend the collegium. It was the regular composition of the collegium, but as far as I remember, Zavisic did not participate in the work of the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me whether chiefs of administrations of the state security department attended the collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Chiefs of administrations of the state security department did not attend the collegium meetings, except for the chief of the state security departments. Chiefs of administrations and other organisational units of the state security department did not participate in the work of the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did the minister issue any tasks to the members of the state security departments at the collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No. The minister did not give any tasks to representatives of the state security departments at the collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Spasic, please tell me, were there any collegium meetings during the NATO aggression, between the 24th of March until the 10th of -- until the 20th of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes. The collegium meetings were held during that time as well, and those who were present varied. It depended who could be present or not, but the meetings were held during the bombing campaign and the aggression. The meetings were held in various locations where the seat of the ministry was located at the moment, but the question was only whether all the members of the collegium would be able to attend the meetings because it depended on the locations where they were deployed at the time. So the meetings were held with many difficulties because the ministry, that is to say the seat of the ministry, was in various locations. There were many problems because of that, but the collegium was active.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what were the problems that the collegium dealt with during 1998 and 1999 until the end of the NATO aggression.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The issues that the collegium dealt with were duties relating to the public security, just like before. That was its responsibility before the NATO aggression and so it was during the aggression, because the life in the republic was continuing normally, or not normally, but it simply continued. And all the problems that existed in the republic before the beginning of the NATO aggression did not cease to exist. I mean crime and everything else. That was why the collegium still dealt with public security issues that it used to deal with before this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me also whether you were informed at these meetings about the general security situation in the republic; and if so, in what way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, there were no special analyses or statements. The minister would give us a general assessment about the situation in the republic and the security in just a few words, and that was all that was discussed at the collegium -- or rather, we did not discuss it, but we just received the minister's statement in the form that he thought was sufficient for a particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss planning and managing anti-terrorist operations or actions in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija at the collegium meetings held in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No, we did not discuss this at the collegium meetings because it was not an issue that we would address at the public security collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you had a chance at these collegium meetings at any time to learn about a report about planned or conducted anti-terrorist operations that were carried out in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No. There was a statement by the minister that a staff had been formed in Kosovo and that it would deal with problems that had to do with the situation in Kosovo. So at the collegium of the public security department, the collegium that I attended, we did not discuss any sort of plans or anti-terrorist operations, or any other problems connected with these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you mention the staff, what sort of information did you receive? What kind of staff was that and what did the minister tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The minister told us that in order to deal with the problems and manage the duties in Kosovo, a staff had been set up, that it would report to him; and that was the information that we had, that he would deal with resolving problems that had to do with Kosovo. He said that it was his decision to set up such a staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at Exhibit P57.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, this is a decision to establish a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism dated the 16th of June, 1998, and on the last page of this decision we can see that it was made by Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. I will ask you to go through this decision with me quickly. As the minister informed you that the staff had been set up, can you please look at the Roman numeral I. It says there: "Head of staff Major-General Sreten Lukic." Which department did Mr. Lukic belong to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: After him, deputy head of the staff is listed, Mr. David Gajic. From which department was Mr. David Gajic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic was a member of the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: If you look, the fourth person listed, assistant head for special operations, Milorad Lukovic. Can you tell me which department Mr. Lukovic came from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic was a member of the state security department. He was the commander of the -- of a state security unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could the chief of the public security department issue any orders to members of the state security department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No. Such a possibility did not exist. Members of the public security department could issue -- could not issue orders to members of the state security department, nor could it happen the other way around. That is to say that each department had its own scope of responsibilities and could not issue orders to members of the other department.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the person that could issue orders to members of both departments?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The only person who could make this decision and issue such decisions was the minister, Vlajko Stojiljkovic, and that is visible because he was the person who appointed the persons listed here. He signed it and he was the only person within the ministry who had the authority to issue orders to both departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please have a look at page 2 of this document, Roman numeral II, which mentions the task of the staff. And can you tell us if this corresponds with the information that you received from the minister or the information that you had.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: This was the task that the staff received from the minister. We did not have information about this nor were we involved in these kind of duties. We did not know what it was. They were authorised by the minister to organise the duties in the way in which the minister defined it here, but we did not have the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at the paragraph marked with the Roman numeral III, and tell me who was the chief -- the head of the staff report to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: As I said, the head of the staff reported to the person who appointed him to this position. And according to this decision, he reports personally to the minister. And he's responsible for his work or the work of the staff directly to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Spasic. Could we please have a look at Exhibit D434. Mr. Spasic, this is a summary from -- of the meeting held in Belgrade on the 16th of October, 1998, between the minister and chiefs of secretariats in Belgrade compiled by the analysis administration. First of all, can you tell me how frequently were the meetings of the minister with the chiefs of secretariats held and was this regular practice?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: It was the usual practice, and the meetings were held every three months. The period between two meetings was three months. That was one of the aspects of our work in which the chiefs of secretariats did participate, so they were organised quarterly at the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you attend such meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What was discussed at such meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The work during the last three months or since the previous meetings was analysed at these meetings. The chiefs of administrations would note the problems that the service had and which had to do with the work of the secretariats. They would also issue instructions to the chiefs of secretariats on how to overcome these problems. So it was an overview of the work between the two collegium meetings, also an overview of the results of the work and the problems that were noted in that specific period which had an impact on the achievement of planned tasks. So the chiefs of secretariats were alerted about all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, were anti-terrorist activities of police forces in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in the given period ever discussed at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No. These meetings, as I said, served to analyse the work by specific duties of the public security department, and there was no analysis of the anti-terrorist operations. We discussed the regular duties that had to do with public security and the problems which arose during the discharging of these duties, particularly the problems that were noted by administrations which co-ordinated the work of all secretariats in the territory of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with what you just told us, could we please have a look at page 8 in the English version of this document, that is to say in the B/C/S version; and page 6 in the English version of this document. Mr. Spasic, this is quite a large document, but I will direct your attention to the section that I managed to find in the document and which treats information that has to do with the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. So can you please have a look at paragraphs 3 and 4 and tell us very briefly, what is the data mentioned in these paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what section you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraphs 3 and 4, the paragraph which begins with: "This year in the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija ..." and the following paragraph which begins with the words: "Terrorist gangs of Albanian separatists..." et cetera.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I cannot find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's a document which is a summary of the minister's meeting with the chief of the secretariats of the 16th of October. If you cannot find it, look at the upper right-hand corner of the Serbian version and you will find page 5. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: So underneath the paragraph "poredne verdene" [phoen] in the overall period. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In the upper right-hand corner you have the number 5, and the paragraph begins: "In this year in the region of AP Kosovo ..."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: We're not able to find where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we don't want to lose precious time, so we will skip that and continue and perhaps we will come back to this later. I'm just going to ask you to tell me this: This meeting and other meetings of that kind, until the end of the NATO aggression, did it ever review any kind of plans for combatting and suppressing terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No, we never did. We mostly had statistical overviews of the events from the sphere of public security. We didn't review any plans, and we really did not deal with those matters at the collegiums. This was an analysis of the work for the previous three months of the work relating to public security, and I have found the paragraph now.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of that, let us just carry on. Let us look at D258, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. This is telegram number 595 of the 22nd of March, 1999, which you sent. Do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, who did you send this telegram to and what does it say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: As you can see from the heading, the telegram was sent to all the secretariats, and it has to do with the preparations of the service for -- this was an additional instruction because we were asking the fire prevention police administration to bring their work up to full alert and what was even more important for us was to prepare all of our resources for the possibility of supplying the population with drinking water. Because our equipment is not suitable for use and transport of drinking water, we asked our cisterns, a certain number of our cisterns, to be chemically treated in such a way that they could then be used to carry drinking water. And this is because we were expecting destruction which would require certain types of equipment in order to clear the debris. Then it was necessary to make sure our equipment was in full working order, and also we would need to use fire-fighting equipment from other facilities and companies that had such equipment so that this equipment could be used when needed. Thus, this is an instruction for the service to prepare for the possible use of equipment that we didn't have but that would be essential for our action in clearing the debris and providing assistance to the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Spasic. For the purposes of the transcript, can you please tell us why was the telegram sent in the first place, preparations for what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: For alleviating the consequences of the NATO bombing, which was expected on the basis of the developments that were occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Spasic. Did you ever go to Kosovo in the period of 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No, I never went there because there was no need for me to go. I had a lot of things to do to organise and prepare the whole service throughout the whole territory of the republic. So at that time I did not go to Kosovo. I didn't even go to the other parts of the republic because there were so many things that we had to do to prepare our equipment. As I said, we had a lot of difficulties because this period was preceded by the period of the embargo when we were not able to procure many things that would have been of assistance to the citizens once the bombing did occur, and this is why we had to invest the utmost effort to bring the service up to scratch in order to be able to work to its best possible potential after and during the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, did you and your administration participate in any kind of anti-terrorist actions or preparations in the territory of Kosovo during 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No. My force did not participate in any kind of action of that type.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what your activities were once the aggression began on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: By its very nature, the service that I was at the head of meant that we were very busy, working hard, in the period when the aggression on our country began. All the operations by the NATO air force were carried out during the night, and because my service had an extremely complex assignment to protect the citizens, the lives of citizens, from the consequences of the NATO bombing, it was our duty to monitor the events. So from the beginning of the bombing until the end, for that period, I spent every night up all night in the headquarters following what was going on throughout the territory of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the places where the seat of the Ministry of Internal Affairs had been located?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Always. I would always be in those locations because I was one of the members of the leadership who spent that entire two-and-a-half-month period working throughout the whole time that the NATO bombing lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us all the locations where the relocated MUP ministry was during the NATO bombing campaign.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Because of the danger of bombing, we would periodically move the headquarters. The first headquarters was located at our sports centre in Makis, then we moved can be then we moved to Studenci Trg square. From there we moved the headquarters to the Partizanski Put company's hostel. After that we went to an elementary school in the Crveni Krst neighbourhood. And after that the last location of the HQ where we spent the longest was at the premises of the Komercijalna Bank in Lola Ivo Ribar Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us who was with you at all of those places?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The chief of the department was with me as well as our colleagues, generals, assistant ministers. I was there every day, every night, and they would switch according to an established rota for the shifts. And during the day they were at the HQ. As I said, I was there every day, and the chief of the department was with me there every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Was the minister there with you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. But he didn't spend his whole time there. He would come and go. The government was working. They had their own work. He would come and he spent quite a lot of time with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about all of these places where you were during the NATO bombing campaign, I'm primarily interested in the way your work was organised in all of those places where you were, how many premises did you have, how was the work organised, how many people were there at all times. Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Well, the space was quite confined. There was one main room where I sat with the assistants and the chief of the department, and there was also the room used by the minister. I failed to mention the chamber of commerce of Serbia as one of the locations where we did spend a lot of time as well, the HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what your role was as the duty officer and who did you maintain contact with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: As the duty officer, it was my duty to keep in touch with all the secretariats -- actually, it was their job to keep in touch with me and to pass on information about the NATO bombing, the number of the projectiles spent, the facilities damaged, and to actually inform me about that after the action was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you communicate with the members of your administration throughout the whole territory of the republic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: For a time, yes. At the beginning while this was possible, to maintain telephone contacts with the secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija, yes. After the lines were cut, we kept in touch with the secretariats in the territory of Serbia and with the secretariat in Pristina. We would receive information about the events in Kosovo through this secretariat in Pristina. The other secretariats had direct contact with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of communications did you have at your disposal as the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I had telephone communications and each time our HQ was relocated, the signals administration or department would set up the communications that we would be using. And then there were also some messengers that we used when we were unable to use regular telephone communications, but we would be immediately informed about events by telephone except for the things that were happening in Kosovo. Because from the point of time when communications were severed because of the bombing, we lost communication with the secretariats in Kosovo and our only communication proceeded through the Pristina secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, did anyone else have telephone communications at their disposal other than yourself at all of these locations where the HQ was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Other than this room where we were on duty, and we had the telephone communications there, the minister also would have his own separate area where he sat and he also had telephone communications at his disposal so that he could communicate with people without us having any information or insight into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The information about the consequences of the NATO forces bombing, was that the only information you received as the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I would only receive information about the effects of the bombing, also about the number of casualties, the number of projectiles. This was the only kind of information that I was receiving.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you make reports on the basis of this information that you received; and if you did, who did you send the reports to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The NATO forces attacks were carried out according to a certain rhythm. They would begin in the evening. The actions for the most part lasted until morning, and after 6.00 a.m. they would stop. I and my colleague who was on the duty shift with me as well as our colleagues from the analysis department, we would all draft a report that was supposed to have been finished sometime by 7.00 a.m. Then we would send this report to the minister, we would send it to the prime minister, and we would send it to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, who was the prime minister and who was the president of the republic at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The prime minister was Mr. Mirko Marjanovic, and the president of the republic was Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, I will show you two documents now and ask you to go through them as quickly as possible. First it's D008-5990. This is an Official Note dated the 30th of March, 1999, from the Pristina secretariat, which talks about the bombing of the SUP building in Pristina and the fact that it burned, together with the inventory and the documents that were in the building. My question for you is if you're familiar with this and if members of your department participated in alleviating the consequences of this incident.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with this. Members of the service that I managed did intervene in order to alleviate the consequences, but when I see the report now it's an Official Note compiled by the people who conducted the on-site investigation after the NATO forces attack. And why I remember this report is because special connections that we had with Pristina were destroyed on this occasion and we could not communicate by these special phones as we call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00927, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see Exhibit D010-0317.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, this is a dispatch number 3024, if I'm not mistaken, dated the 3rd of April, 1999, which talks about the bombing of buildings of the federal and republican Ministry of the Interior in Kneza Milosa Street in Belgrade. It was compiled by the head of duty shift, Major Strahinja Petrovic. I wonder if you're familiar with any of the details about incident, and if so, what. But please be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I'm absolutely familiar with this incident, because immediately after the NATO air force attack on our building I went to the site, and I managed the operation to extinguish the fire. The chief of the department and myself came to the site immediately. I co-ordinated the work, and as this was a huge fire, because incendiary ordnance was used in this attack, quite a lot of forces that we had in Belgrade participated in extinguishing this particular fire. We also used the assistance of the public utilities company, which helped us with water cisterns, and we used the assistance of military fire-fighting units. The fire was big on two facilities of special interest, and three members of the fire-fighting department were injured, not seriously. They were released from hospital quickly. But we came to the site very quickly, the chief of the department and myself. And the minister and other top-ranking officials came there very quickly as well. But as I said, the fire spread across a big part of the building and destroyed a lot of materiel and documents which were stored in the SUP building. Incendiary bombs fell on the republican SUP building, whereas the federal SUP building was attacked by destructive bombs. So it was destroyed because it toppled, whereas the building of the republican SUP burned. That was why we had to engage very strong forces to extinguish the fire in this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Spasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00928, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see Exhibit D254.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, it is a dispatch number 10 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not catch the number and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see this dispatch in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 4th of May, 1999, that's the right dispatch. Can you please tell me if you're familiar with this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am because together with the chief of the department I prepared it for the ground, and I sent it when it was signed by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm particularly interested in the dispatch is on page 2 in both versions. That's paragraph 3 in the Serbian version, which says: "If it is assessed that -- if there is information or assessment that the aggressor could attack again, organise interventions so that those who will participate in extinguishing the fire and the equipment would not be in jeopardy, but they should be close to the site and ready for intervention." Can you tell us, what was the reason for this instruction?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the NATO attacks, the minister requested that in certain facilities such as the building of the republican SUP, I should deploy forces so that there would be -- right there at the site. I did not do that, and I suffered certain consequences afterwards. But it turned out that that was justified, I mean not to send the forces to the very location that was expected to be a target of the bombing. And this dispatch is a consequence of the attack on the federal Ministry of Defence when our employees started the intervention at the request of the minister. And then there was another attack and 12 firefighters were seriously injured on that occasion, four vehicles were destroyed. And therefore, in agreement with the chief of the department, I prepared this dispatch and he sent it out to our organisational units. He said there that people and equipment should be saved and that they should only intervene when they were certain that there -- the conditions were good for a safe intervention. Because as I said, 12 people were seriously injured and four vehicles were completely destroyed because there was a repeated attack after the intervention had started, because the NATO attack had not stopped, and the lives of our men were threatened because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at Exhibit D008-6697.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, just briefly, this is an overview of the attacks carried out by the NATO Pact in the period between the 24th of March and the 2nd of May, 1999. Roads are mentioned. Can you tell me if you're familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Was this document drawn up on the basis of information which you received as the duty officer at the minister HQ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: This is an amalgamated document which lists all the incidents that we registered in the reports that we were receiving from the ground in this period, and it corresponds with the reports which I was receiving in this period on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Spasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00929, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would ask to have the break now and I would need just a short period after the break with a few questions for this witness so that I ensure that my learned friends from the OTP have sufficient time for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Popovic. Mr. Spasic, we have a break now for technical reasons, and it will also give you an opportunity to rest for a little while. We resume in one half an hour, that is in a half-hour from now, just after 11.00. If you could be ready, we will continue at that time and Mr. Popovic will continue with his questions. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I see you're ready, Mr. Spasic, and Mr. Popovic will now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, we will continue. Can we please look at Exhibit D011-5115. Mr. Spasic, that is the last document in your binder. The title of the document is the overview of the attacks of the NATO Alliance on the Republic of Serbia from the 24th of March until the 11th of June, 1999. First of all, are you familiar with this document and can we see the following page, please. Could you please look at the next page. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the next page, we can see in the columns the time, place, the facility, number of projectiles, the consequences and the intervention. These are the headings of the columns. Is this the type of information that you received from the members of your administration as the duty operations officer at the relocated ministry HQ?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive all this information because in dealing with the consequences of these events, the members of the service that I was at the head of were involved and I received all this information. This is the information relevant for that mentioned period. If you look at the last column, interventions, you can see that team 93 participated in each of those interventions, and that is actually the service of which I was chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In order to confirm what you are saying, I would just like to ask to look at page 18 in the B/C/S and page 8 in the English. This is an overview of the NATO Pact attacks on the territory of the Republic of Serbia at 1445 hours on the 2nd of April until the 3rd of April, 1999. We are looking at this document on our monitor. Sir, have you managed to find it in your binder?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the 3rd, 4th, to the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, from the 2nd of April, 1445 hours, until the 4th of April at 0510 hours -- the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you look at column 30050, Belgrade, the building of the republican MUP, major materiel damage, two firefighters injured during their intervention. Is this what we were talking about earlier and is that the type of information that you were receiving?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. It's just that I think that there were more projectiles -- actually, there were three projectiles which hit the building of the republican SUP and one that hit the building of the federal SUP. But, yes, I do remember that incident in exceptional detail because after the actual strike I was there together with the chief of the department. And so we already knew what this was about even without this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is a different document, is it, Mr. Popovic, from the one we received just before the break? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, precisely. The document that we looked at before the break had to do with the communications, rail traffic, road traffic, and roads. And this refers to the events on the territory of the whole republic during the NATO bombing campaign, and the strikes are referred to here. So it contains a little bit more detailed information than the document that we looked at before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00930, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, did you see General Djordjevic in the course of 1999 in the period from the beginning of the NATO aggression, the 24th of March, until the withdrawal of the forces from Kosovo and Metohija, which was on the 10th of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I pointed out already several times that I saw him on a daily basis. Perhaps once or twice for different reasons also, but I would see him every day because every evening we would sit and decide who would be on duty with me, who would be assisting me in my work during the night. So this was a daily contact that we had. I think once or twice, if I can remember correctly, that I did not see him, perhaps one or two days I did not see him. Otherwise, our contact was every day because the two of us would make the schedule of those who would be working during the day to compile the information that was arriving from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you saw him every day, can you tell us where you saw him, where was it that you saw him every day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: We saw each other at all the locations where the HQ was located, wherever it was that the HQ was operating from he would be in the same operations room that I was in. This applied to all the locations that I referred to where the staff was located during the NATO bombing campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Which town are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Belgrade, right next to me. I did not leave Belgrade throughout that whole period and he was right there with me, at the same location where the HQ of the ministry was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, did you go out to the actual sites of the NATO bombing attacks where the bombing strikes occurred during the bombing -- NATO bombing campaign?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Of course. We very often went to the sites, especially if special, important facilities were involved or facilities where there were victims or civilian buildings where it was necessary to organise an effective protection for the endangered civilians, perhaps next to the republican and the federal MUP buildings. For example, we would go together with General Vlastimir Djordjevic to the secretariat for National Defence, that ministry; then we would go together where the maternity clinic of the Dragisa Misovic hospital was struck where there were some casualties too, and where the small children and the women who were there were in danger. Then we also went to the gynaecology clinic, where we had to take measures in order to protect the women there because that hospital building is quite close to the republican SUP building. So the secondary activities which were a consequence of the strikes at the SUP building would be affecting the maternity clinic as well. So General Djordjevic and I went there to see that maternity clinic, to determine the degree of danger, and to devise measures in order to help the victims, the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, during the NATO bombing campaign, since you were at the HQ of the MUP that was relocated, what was the main preoccupation of the chief of the department, and generally the main preoccupation of the public security department chief during the NATO bombing campaign?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Their main preoccupation and their focus of interest, both of the chief of the department and myself and all the other chiefs of departments, was to help the threatened population because the attacks were quite barbaric, conducted with rocket ordnance and missiles. So there was no way to help the population in any other way, except to organise direct evacuation and to organise conditions for them to condition with their lives, to help them. So that was one of the main activities that the chief of the department was dealing with other than his regular duties, that I was really not knowledgeable about. By the very nature of his post, he was the one in charge of dealing with the effects of the bombing campaign, and together with him because he was my superior and had greater authorities, together with him we would take measures to help the endangered population that had found itself in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the purposes of the transcript, line 18 should state administration instead of department. That's the first word. Mr. Spasic, when you talked about the locations where the MUP HQ was, can you please tell me whether General Djordjevic had a separate office, an office of his own in those places.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No, he did not because it wasn't possible to provide him with that. It was not possible to have separate offices. There was just one central, main room where all the activities were being organised and executed. It was an HQ. And the only isolated area was the area allocated to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether Mr. Djordjevic had his own telephone line, separate telephone line?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. Nobody had a separate telephone line except the minister. We all used the same telephone line which was installed in the operations room where we were on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me, when you were there were you ever present when Mr. Djordjevic spoke with the HQ for the suppression of terrorist activities in Kosovo and General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I can state with quite a high degree of certainty that he did not because I would be the first one to pick up the phone and I never responded -- picked up the phone when General Lukic would be at the other end. So during the time that I was present - and that was for most of the day every day - I can say that they did not have contact together, at least not when I was there. It would be quite probable that if they were having regular contact, I would have picked up the phone at least once when that occurred. And as far as I know, this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, what was your impression, what was the relationship between General Djordjevic and the minister of the interior, Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: It's my impression -- and not just my impression, it was evident that their relations were quite cool.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And at the end, did you ever in the course of 1998 or 1999 hear that there was any kind of plan or agreement in the Ministry of the Interior, whereby the Albanian population in Kosovo would be expelled from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I never saw or heard anything like that, and I don't think that such a plan existed because this is something that I would have known for sure. As an argument for this assertion of mine that such a plan did not exist, I can say that in the service that I was heading there were many Albanians in a lot of these places. And had there been any tendencies or aspirations to eliminate them, definitely this would have happened in my service as well because they occupied some pretty high-ranking positions. So they would have been removed from my service as well. I am sure that there were no such plans present in the ministry that I knew about. I didn't know of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you're talking about members of the Albanian ethnic minority who were employed in your administration, could you please tell us which posts there were, and what are the people that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the commander of the firefighters' unit in Pec, he was an Albanian. The chief of the division in -- of the fire-fighting division in Prizren was also an Albanian. In Pristina there were several department commanders who were Albanians and who worked together the whole time. So I think that there was no location in Kosovo where my service was active without having Albanians as part of the staff. There were no differences or divisions as far as employment was concerned. And stating this with full responsibility. They had equal status with all the other members of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see in the course of 1998 or 1999 that there was any kind of plan or agreement within the Ministry of Internal Affairs which would seek to change the ethnic structure in Kosovo by expelling the Albanian minority population from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I never heard of such a plan and such a plan was never reviewed in our department when I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Spasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am now ending my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Popovic. Ms. -- yes, Ms. Gopalan. There will be some questions for you now, Mr. Spasic, by Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, you said today that the minister did not give any tasks to representatives of the RDB at the collegium. Now, these were the head of the RDB, Rade Markovic; and his deputy, Mr. Curcic. Now, do you recall saying that, that the minister didn't issue tasks to reps of the RDB at the collegiums?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He did not issue any assignments to representatives of the RDB.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are you then suggesting that the minister had no authority to issue tasks to RDB representatives?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that because I already pointed out that the minister was superior, both to the public security and the state security department. But the specific nature of the duties of those two departments were not compatible in order to be able to issue orders at a meeting like this to the state security department. I assume that the minister -- actually, the minister probably did issue assignments to them at other types of meetings which would not be reviewed at the collegium. The topic of review at the collegium would be matters relating to public security. So for that reason, he would be issuing orders only to us, not to them, because this collegium dealt with public security matters in the republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, so you're saying that because the collegium dealt with matters of public security, the minister was not able to issue tasks to the members of the RDB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that he was not able to, but that he didn't have any need to do that at these particular meetings because those assignments had nothing to do with the type of public security jobs that we were performing, that we were executing, and that we were responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recall saying that the minister set up the MUP staff because he was the only one with authority to issue orders to the RDB and the RJB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes. By law the minister was the person officially in charge of both those departments, and he would be the only one who could issue documents of that nature which would be applied in both the departments. He did have that authority as minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you then explain what seems to be a contradiction to me. Now, you say that by law the minister was officially in charge of both departments, but you say that he was only able to issue orders in the context of the MUP staff but not to members of the MUP collegium who were RDB members. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I did not say that in that way, that he was the only one who could issue that. I mean, they were responsible to him, but I did not say that in this particular way that you said it. I was not interpreted correctly if it came out that way. I did not say that. The minister could issue orders to both of the departments, but when we were having that meeting, the collegium meeting, this was a collegium which reviewed the work problems from the public security service sphere.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, you also said that it was the minister's decision to set up the MUP staff. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, the minister issued a decision to form the staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know that prior to the minister's decision, Mr. Djordjevic had also issued a decision to set up -- or establish the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Djordjevic, the chief of the department, did not make a decision on the forming of the MUP staff. I think that that was the staff of the public security department, which he was authorised to do and that he was in charge of. And he was authorised to issue that kind of decision. I didn't see the document, but I know that the chief of the department did issue a decision on the forming of the staff of the public security staff, not the MUP staff. MUP would encompass both of these departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, the public security department is also part of the MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I pointed out that the MUP comprises two departments: The public security department and the state security department. Mr. Djordjevic was authorised to issue orders which were valid for the members of the public security department. And a decision which he made to set up a staff implied members of the public security department who were supposed to discharge duties from the remit of work of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And do you know that in appointing and setting up this staff, Mr. Djordjevic also appointed Mr. Lukic as the head of the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I have not seen that decision, but if that is what the decision says, Mr. Djordjevic had the right -- I'm not sure, who do you mean he appointed as the head of the staff? Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes. I said Mr. Lukic was appointed as head of the MUP staff by Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic is a member of the public security department. He was an assistant in the city secretariat of the interior, and as a member of the public security department he could have been appointed as head of the staff by Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan, just to ensure that my understanding is correct and the transcript can be understood correctly, when you refer to the MUP staff are you referring to that staff established essentially in Pristina dealing with anti-terrorist activities?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
