utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems to me that everything was clear until you asked this question just now. I would kindly ask Ms. Gopalan to be specific as to the staff which she has in mind and to mention the date when it was set up, because it was not the staff for the prevention of terrorist activities which Mr. Djordjevic set up. There was no such staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is one of those issues which I'm sure we will hear much about, Mr. Popovic. But as I understand, there were decisions approximately a week apart in June of 1998. Are we on the right track?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, having regard to what we have discussed so far in relation to this MUP staff, you would agree with me then when you said that it was the minister's decision to set up this MUP staff, this was not an entirely accurate statement? Sir, did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: It was a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've discussed Mr. Djordjevic's involvement in setting up a MUP staff. Now, having had this discussion, you would agree with me, then, that when you said the minister made the decision to set up the MUP staff, this statement was not entirely accurate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I repeat, the minister issued a decision to set up the MUP staff. If you have a look at the personnel, the staff included representatives of both public and state security departments, and only the minister could do that. Mr. Djordjevic could not have set up such a staff. It was only the minister who could set it up because the staff included the representatives from both departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: We'll leave that for now, sir. Now, in 1998 would you agree with me that the situation -- the security situation in Kosovo was a complex one?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in 1999 the security situation in Kosovo was also complex; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In fact, Kosovo was in the forefront of the NATO attacks; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with that. According to the data that we have, the entire republic was exposed to NATO attacks. It was not that Kosovo was at the forefront. If you analyse the information that we received from the ground, the picture that we get about the attacks is that they were equally distributed throughout the republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So Kosovo was also a victim, so to speak, of the NATO attacks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The statistics that we kept and judging by the incidents in Kosovo, yes, Kosovo suffered as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, the security situation in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999 was within the remit of responsibility of the public security department; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: It was within the remit of work of the Ministry of the Interior. I could not say who particularly was responsible because the responsibility was not defined in such a way that the public security department was in charge of the security situation in Kosovo. It was part of the responsibility of the Ministry of the Interior. It was responsible for the security situation in the whole republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that the RJB was responsible for sending policemen to Kosovo to deal with the security situation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The public security department was responsible for sending policemen and organising police service in the entire republic, not just in Kosovo. So as it sent policemen to Kosovo, it sent them and deployed them in other areas of the republic. It was responsible for the operation of police in other parts of the republic, not just in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, just focusing on Kosovo, do you know that around 14.000 MUP personnel were sent to Kosovo by the RJB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this information. As I was doing very specific segment of work and I was not in touch with the organisation of the police service, I cannot talk about these numbers because that was not part of my remit of work. I did not have such information, and I was not interested in information relating to the part of service that had nothing to do with me. I was facing numerous problems, and I had a lot to do that had to do with the security of the citizens of Serbia, so I did not have enough time to take into account all the numbers, and I am not familiar with these particular figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, a question about the MUP collegiums. Now, you would agree with me that apart from the Minister Stojiljkovic, the assistant ministers, so Mr. Markovic, for example, and Mr. Djordjevic, were very high-ranking MUP members who attended the collegiums.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, you have said that anti-terrorist operations were not discussed during MUP collegiums; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, I've already given you the number of units that were involved at ground level in Kosovo. Now, do you know that the MUP collegium also dealt with requests for replenishing units in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The MUP collegium did not deal with the number of units or the number of the members of units that were sent to Kosovo. At the MUP collegium meetings we discussed the logistics necessary to discharge these duties, and that was the necessary equipment, accommodation, transportation, and everything else. But as for these numbers, that was not discussed at the collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And you also discussed the requests for troop rotations at these meetings, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I do not know that that was discussed, and this is a statement that I cannot confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Well, we've heard testimony in this courtroom that this was a matter that was discussed during MUP collegiums. Now, having regard to these matters that were discussed in the collegium that you say, the logistics, the necessary equipment that had to be sent, do you also know that these issues were permanently on the agenda of the MUP collegium in order to monitor the situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I never said that that was on the agenda. I'm not sure where you received this information, that this was on the agenda regularly. I don't remember it. We did not receive such information and especially not regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, we have heard testimony from Mr. Misic, so your direct superior, that questions relating to logistical requests, the reinforcement and engagement of units, were constantly on the agenda because there was no other way for us to monitor the current situation in Kosmet. This is at T14087 for my learned counsel's reference. Now, what I'd like to know is: Do you remember these matters being discussed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I repeat, I do not remember this, and it was not something I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: In my work-plan, I did not have anything connected with this. I don't remember it. This is the first time I hear that these figures and the fact that they were discussed. Because I wish to note also that that was 12 years ago, and for me to remember something that happened 12 years ago, particularly figures, especially as I'm convinced that I would remember at least some of it, I don't remember that this was discussed at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, you started off by saying that anti-terrorist operations were not discussed during MUP collegiums. Now, I've given you some examples of matters relating to anti-terrorist operations that were discussed in the MUP collegium. Now, is it your testimony that you had this information in terms of the logistics of the units on the ground but no one spoke about what these units were actually doing during these collegiums, that you didn't discuss the security operations in Kosovo. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I declare that there was no discussion about any anti-terrorist activities at the collegium meetings. And as for logistics, that was normal because it was necessary to justify the costs and to state what they were. But as for the anti-terrorist activities themselves, I assert that that was not discussed at all at the collegium meetings because the composition of the collegium was such that it was very varied, both in professional terms and in terms of the problems that it could deal with, so that there was no discussion of anti-terrorist activities. That's what I repeat. And at least I'm not aware of that. If somebody else was present when it was discussed -- though I think I attended all the collegium meetings, and I think that there was never any discussion of such anti-terrorist activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've already spoken about the composition of the collegium, and you've said that there was no dispute about the fact that a number of the collegium members were extremely high-ranking members of the MUP. Now, sir, we have a very complex security situation, a very serious situation. We have high-ranking members of the police meeting to discuss the logistics relating to the security situation. But your testimony is that these high-ranking MUP officials failed to discuss any matter relating to what these MUP units did in Kosovo. You were just interested in the cost implications of sending troops to Kosovo. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I'm saying what I know about the whole situation. There was no discussion about anti-terrorist activities at these MUP meetings. I think that professionally speaking this is not done in plenary session, which are attended by other representatives of services that have nothing to do with such areas of work. This is why I still assert that I was not present at the collegium meetings where such issues were discussed. They were not discussed at the collegium meetings that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, of the collegium meetings that were held, how many did you actually attend?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: All the meetings that were held on Mondays or Tuesdays that I was invited to attend by the minister's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So you're saying that these matters could have been discussed in meetings that you did not attend?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: But it doesn't necessarily mean that these were the collegium meetings. I said that anti-terrorist activities were not discussed at the collegium meetings, and I have no other information about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were also asked today about a meeting that took place in October 1998, and this is D434, that's the exhibit number. And it was a meeting between the minister and the SUP chiefs. Do you recall talking about this meeting today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, my understanding of what you said about this meeting -- and just to set some context is that this was a meeting attended by high-ranking members of the RJB, including Mr. Djordjevic. Now, you said that anti-terrorist activities of the police forces were not discussed at these meetings. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I see my learned colleague on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that, but I'm waiting for you to finish this particular line of questioning, Ms. Gopalan. Is it a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to clarify and because of the question that is asked, if we look at this document, Mr. Djordjevic was not present at the meeting. This may help with the precision of the question and what might ensue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it's also a matter that can be dealt with in re-examination, Mr. Popovic. We want to get through this evidence quickly today, and I think most of your interventions are matters that you can deal with in re-examination. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question, sir. Now, this was a meeting attended by high-ranking members of the RJB, and now you said that anti-terrorist activities were not discussed at this meeting and such meetings. Is that correct, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you saying that Mr. Djordjevic did not attend other meetings with other high-ranking MUP officials where anti-terrorist operations were discussed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I don't know if there were such meetings and if he attended them because I did not attend them nor was I invited to such meetings. Therefore, I cannot say whether he attended any such meetings or not. This is a question to which I cannot answer because I did not attend them. I have already replied that at the meetings that I attended, such as these, anti-terrorist activities were not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Now, what were all the kinds of meetings that were held by the minister or somebody else, this is something I don't know. I'm just responding about the meetings that I did attend.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In that case, sir, so you don't know anything about a meeting attended by Mr. Djordjevic in Belgrade in late October with the MUP leadership, including President Milosevic, where anti-terrorist operations were discussed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I'm not a MUP official of such a high rank that I would know where my superiors are, let alone when they had meetings with officials higher than those who were my immediate superiors, neither do I know that there was such a meeting, nor who chaired it, nor who attended it. This is the first time I hear of this meeting because I was not of such a rank where I would be informed about such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've said that you were of not such a high rank that you would be aware of meetings attended by your superiors. Now, following on from that, did you attend any meetings in which anti-terrorist operations were planned?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No, I never attended such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Did you receive --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Nor did I know that they were held or if they were held at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And I take it then, based on your answer, that you were not informed about the results of such meetings after they had completed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No, because the topics were probably not of interest for my service and nobody felt that any personnel from my service would be required in these activities. So this is probably why I did not take part in the meetings either.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And so, sir, you kept yourself busy then with matters relating to your line of work, so fire-fighting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Not fire-fighting only, but also fire-fight -- anti-fire-fighting measures as well. Fire-fighting is only just one aspect of that particular service.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've also said that you were not interested in matters that had nothing to do with you. Do you recall saying that just slightly earlier today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, since you were not a high-ranking MUP official and you kept yourself busy with matters relating to your line of work and that you also did not attend meetings in which anti-terrorist operations were planned, now having all that in mind you would not have known about any plan to expel if there had been one; correct? You wouldn't have seen one because it was outside your line of work.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No, no, I wouldn't have. It was outside of my line of work, and I didn't know of such plans, nor did I take part in actions provided for under such plans, either myself or members of my service. So I don't know absolutely that such plan exist, nor did I participate in any way in the discussion about them, the preparations for such plans, or the implementation of such plans, and neither did I know they existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, at the time of the NATO bombing, could you clarify for me the number of telephones that were functioning in your headquarters that you were based at in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: We had a telephone through which we received information from the field, and there was also a telephone that the minister had at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So there were two telephones that were functioning at your headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many were working. I'm talking about two that we used.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So you had access to two telephones at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: We -- I actually had access to just one telephone, through which I received information. The access to the other phone was only for the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And there were no cell phones available?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: There were cell phones, but we had banned them because they could have been used to guide projectiles to strike our facilities. There was a ban on using mobile phones at locations where the HQ was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I see. Now, sir, the information that you received through this telephone that you had access to -- and I think you said today that: "We would be immediately informed about events by telephone, except for what was happening in Kosovo." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me see if I understand this evidence correctly. We've already established early on that there is a war going on; correct? Sir, did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: You agree with me --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No, could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I will, sir. Now, at this time there was a war going on; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And as you mentioned earlier, the bombing affected both Kosovo and Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And you'd agree that this would be a pretty serious situation for a country to be in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And that this situation had been prompted by events in Kosovo, that the NATO bombing had been prompted by events in Kosovo; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have an answer to that. That is not a question, it's an assertion, why did they bomb us. I believe that they had no reason to bomb us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question, sir, in that case. Now, given the centrality of the Kosovo situation to the NATO bombardment, how is it that you did not receive information about what was happening in Kosovo when you had information about other areas? That doesn't strike me as being logical.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that in the way that you are trying to interpret what I said. We received information in the shortest possible period after the events about the consequences of the bombing in the territory of the republic, except from Kosovo. The information about the effects of the bombing in Kosovo would only arrive from Pristina. This information was most often sent by messenger to Pristina, and then only was it passed on to us from Pristina. So we would be receiving this information with a delay, not for any other particular reason, but because technically this was not possible. I have to explain the whole situation. Fire stations were places where people were on duty round the clock, and these fire stations were not exposed to the actions of the NATO forces. They all had regular telephone lines with us, through the post office. But when the MUP centre was destroyed and when the telephone exchange in Kosovo was destroyed, we could no longer have direct communication with our units. The only option was that one link with Pristina. All the information from Kosovo would flow to Pristina, and then from Pristina would be sent to our staff. From other places other than Pristina, information would be sent by messenger.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, we've heard testimony in this case that mobile phones were used by the units in Kosovo during the war. Now, given the importance of having information on what was happening in Kosovo, why is it you received this information with a delay, compared to the other sources of information you had?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I don't know of any kind of method whereby information was received through mobile telephones, and I repeat that we had banned the use of mobile phones in our facilities in order to prevent them from being used to guide missiles. And I repeat that I did not hear of any instances of information being relayed to us through mobile phones. We didn't have mobile phones in our staff. And in our units mobile phones were not used to maintain a line of communication with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, a witness who testified here, Mr. Trajkovic, said that mobile phones were not usually used during the war - this is at T9090 - but it was used for passing on very important and short information, as they didn't have any other means of communication when they were in the field, so when the units were in the field. Now, did you know about that, that this was a form of communication that was available?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No. I am not aware of that, and I did not use this method of communication. I didn't have any need to use this method of communication because the information that I required I would receive via a land-line, and I would use that information received through the land-line. In my work we did not go into the field. We had our duty shifts at the fire stations, and they used land-lines to convey information to us. They didn't have any need to use mobile phones for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, those are all my questions for you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gopalan. Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to be very brief. I would like to ask to see P760, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if Mr. Spasic can see this document. These are documents that the Prosecution said that they would use in their cross-examination today. Mr. Spasic, do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I'm just looking for the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If I may assist, I think it's tab 22 in the witness's binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, this is a document of the 11th of June. It's signed by assistant chief of the public security department, assistant minister, and can you please tell us what it says.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch what the witness read. Could he please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit P50 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's an answer been missed, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, I'm going to repeat my question. This is a document of the 11th of June, signed by assistant minister, chief of the public security department. And can you please read the title of this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The document in front of me, if that's the document that you're referring to, is the decision on the composition of the staff, leaders and members of the staff of the Ministry of the Interior of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And our -- is anti-terrorism or suppression of terrorism mentioned anywhere in this heading of this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit P57, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can you read this decision of the 16th of June, adopted by Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic, can you please read the heading of this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The decision -- the document is: The decision to establish a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, who issued the decision on the establishment of the ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: This decision was issued by Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. That is precisely this one that we have read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question, Mr. Spasic. If logistical matters were to be discussed that you said were discussed at the collegium, could you please tell us which administrations would be in charge with these -- of dealing with these matters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The administration -- the police administration, and the common affairs administration would be in charge of those matters. They were in charge of seeing to the needs of all the organisational units, so this would be the administration for general affairs would be fulfilling the requests of specific administrations. Actually, one of the administrations that also was dealing with logistical matters would be the police administration; they would submit a request to the general affairs administration, asking them to provide the means for them to be able to have the means to fulfil their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And who would approve the requests to these administrations and issue permission for these administrations to meet the requests?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The exclusive right to decide on such requests, whether to accept or deny these requests, lay with the minister. The minister was the only authorised person who could make decisions on requests of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am finished with my re-direct with this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, I have a couple of very short questions. You told us that your direct superior was the assistant minister, Major-General Stojan Misic. Could you tell us who was the direct superior of this person, of Stojan Misic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Stojan Misic's immediate supervisor was the assistant minister by the nature of his function as well as the chief of the administration and then the minister -- actually, the minister was the superior to all the assistant ministers. They were carrying out the duties of assistance to the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that. You were referring to Mr. Djordjevic when you told us his immediate superior was the assistant minister as the chief of administration, the administration for public security I think; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: The tasks covered by Mr. Stojan Misic were in the sphere of public security. So that is why I thought that he was in some way responsible for his work to Mr. Djordjevic, but by the nature of his position and his work he was actually responsible to the minister, Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Who was the deputy of Mr. Djordjevic as head of the public security administration?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I don't know of such a position, the public security administration. I know the public security department and Mr. Djordjevic as the head of the -- the chief of that department did not have a deputy. There was no deputy provided for a chief of the department in the public security department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And in case of his absence, who stood in for him? Who carried out his duties?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: If he was absent, nobody stood in for him, nobody actually carried out his duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us that you received orders from the Minister Stojiljkovic directly. Did you inform your directly superior, Mr. Misic or Mr. Djordjevic, about these duties issued by the minister to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: No, because it was not customary if I received a direct order from the minister for me to interpret his order to others. Because if you would respect the hierarchy, his order was -- if it was done according to the proper hierarchy, I would receive the order from my immediate superior. But in this case, I would directly inform the minister about the results that I achieved while executing the order that I had received directly from him, from the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were your direct superiors satisfied with this situation? It is quite unusual that the direct superior doesn't know about such an order given by a more high-ranking official, like a minister.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I cannot be the judge of that. I'm just saying how we worked. I don't know if they accepted that or not. There was no comment from them. I assume that it was an agreement amongst them that the minister could in some way -- I don't know how their relationship was, how it was. But it was a fact that when the minister issued an order to me, he asked me to inform him back about it personally, and I was not authorised to convey his orders or to inform others about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw this morning some documents, some lists, of damaged facilities because of the NATO bombing, the documents D929 and D930. Did they include also damaged facilities in Kosovo or only in Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I think that all the facilities were throughout the entire Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you -- from your recollection, can you tell us which kind of facilities were listed in these lists primarily.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: For the most part, these were infrastructure facilities, civilian facilities, including hospitals even, as well as industrial facilities which were working for the needs of -- and we described that as special-purpose production, for the needs of the army. They would be manufacturing special-purpose products for the army. They would be damaged, but then a lot of the neighbouring facilities such as roads and bridges were also exposed. One such facility is the maternity clinic in the centre of Belgrade that was also struck. There was a whole series of such objects. There was no selection or differentiation in making these strikes. It was difficult to guess the criteria according to which these targets were picked. The television Belgrade building, some housing, civilian facilities, and then maternity clinics, and some other facilities which by any criteria would not be selected as targets, but these were just facilities that were intended only for civilian use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Spasic, I have understood from your evidence that during the NATO bombing, fire prevention and assistance to the members of the public in respect of the damage from the bombing was one of your primary responsibilities. Do I correctly understand that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was precisely my duty throughout the bombing campaign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it from what you have indicated that the fire-fighting units of the ministry throughout the republic reported to you all bomb damage that occurred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the assessed damage because there was a huge number of attacks on all kinds of property, and the procedure for assessing actual damage requires a lot of time. This was just the first information that we received, the assessment of damage rather than the actual damage. The actual damage was much greater, and we managed to ascertain this information only later on after the on-site investigations had been conducted. This was just the information that stated the number of incidents, the kind of facilities, and the number of projectiles that were used. As for the consequences and the amount of damage, we established that later on through separate on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand that one of your functions then and one of the functions of your organisation was to prepare a report by 7.00 a.m. each day of the effect of the night's bombing throughout the republic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes. The bombing would stop after 6.00 a.m., and with the members of the analysis administration who were on duty at all times I would compile this report, and at 7.00 a.m. I would give it to the minister, and a courier would bring it to the prime minister and the president of the republic. So that was the time by which we would conclude our reports for the previous 24-hour period and then we would dispatch them to the said addresses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And to assist you with that, your units throughout the republic would telephone in to you damage as soon as they could after there was a bombing incident?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you're familiar with the work of fire-fighting units, then you must know that their composition includes communications centres which are manned permanently by crews which have continuous connection with the relevant bodies, and these crews would inform us immediately about the facilities that were targeted and the number of projectiles that hit them. Then later on, as I said, we would establish the amount of damage, and the duty officer was immediately informed about an incident, especially if intervention units were to be sent there. So we had practically immediate information about any incident and all the information -- all the interventions were reported to the duty officer, who would send the intervention unit to the ground. And then when he received information from such an intervention unit, he would inform us about everything that was of interest for us; and then we would further inform our leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you had land-line communication with each of these communication centres of the fire-fighting service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat what I said. We had communication with all centres until the moment when the post office in Pristina was destroyed. After that, we only had communication with Pristina and not with other areas in Kosovo. We did have communication with other centres in the Republic of Serbia proper, and as for the other areas in Kosovo we received information via Pristina because the only telephone line that still operated was the line between Pristina and Belgrade. Therefore, the centre in Pristina was informed about the incidents throughout Kosovo, and then the centre from Pristina forwarded the information to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How many communications centres were there of the fire-fighting service in Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the number because I do not remember, but I can say that every populated place that had more than 10.000 inhabitants had to have a fire-fighting unit and a communications centre as an integral part of it. So all such places were able to inform us about incidents in their area through these communications centre. Each populated place that had more than 10.000 inhabitants had to have such ability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps you could help me, is that likely to be more than 20 communications centres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Many more because we had 33 secretariats in the territory of the republic, so there must have been many more. Each secretariat covered several populated places that had more than 10.000 inhabitants, and each fire-fighting unit had such a centre. I couldn't say how many there were at the time, but there were many more. So 33 secretariats means that there were many more communications centres that were used by the fire-fighting service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And from what you were saying, it would be your primary role each night during the bombing to man the telephone at the headquarters to receive these reports; is that what was happening, you were on duty virtually every night?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Precisely. I was the only high-ranking MUP official who was on duty every night and collected this information and co-ordinated the work of the service on the territory of the entire republic. The co-ordination was very important. There were fires, such as attacks on oil refineries, that required very complex interventions and a large number of troops. I was the one who co-ordinated these forces. So for two and a half months, I never missed a single night when I was not on duty and did not collect the information from the entire republic. The information flowed to where I was stationed, and together with the personnel from the analysis administration I prepared the report so that it would be ready by 7.00 a.m., which was the dead-line set for this information to be sent out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And from what you've been saying, do I understand correctly that your location had to move many times to avoid the risk of bombing to your own location to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes. We changed a number of locations in the city which were unknown and had not been announced to anyone in advance. And as soon as it was possible to move in and for these facilities to be used, we would transfer to a new location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to remember roughly how many different locations you were in during the bombing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: If you followed my testimony, I mentioned precisely all the locations, and I can repeat. The first location was at the MUP sports centre; the second location was at Studenci Trg in Belgrade; the third location was at single-man's hostel; the fourth location was at the chamber of commerce of Serbia; and the fifth location was at the Komercijalna Banka, a bank in Belgrade. These were the locations where we were stationed in these two and a half months. We spent the longest period of time at Komercijalna Banka because this is where we stayed until the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it was a matter of finding a location where it would be possible to accommodate the headquarters staff; is that what was necessary?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: We looked out for locations. While we were at one location, there was a specific service that would find the following location and prepare the logistics for our work there. That implied the telephone lines and everything else that is necessary for a longer stay. In these premises, someone would be staying and working for 24 hours a day. That means that the next location was always prepared in advance. There was a particular service that did that. When it was assessed that the location that we were using at the moment was not safe anymore, we would transfer to a new location that was technically equipped so that the staff could continue with its work there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How big was the staff that moved to these different buildings? Would it be 20 people or 100 people or 300 people? Can you give me some idea.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Between 15 and 20 people served at the headquarters. And members of the headquarters, these were all assistant ministers, all chiefs of departments, the minister, the head of his office, representatives of the analysis administration which -- who helped us with records. There were communications experts who enabled the work of the communications system, and also the personnel who made it possible for us to stay there in terms of hygiene and various technical matters, because we stayed there 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the communications system you mentioned, was there radio communication as well as telephone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: We only used telephone communication because radio communication was very vulnerable, in the sense that it could be bombed. That was why we only used telephone lines, land-lines. I already noted that the use of mobile phones was prohibited and so was the use of any kind of radio equipment. We only used the land-line telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you could be at a location for some weeks before moving from what you're saying; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SPASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We spent up to two weeks in some of the locations, and in some others only for a few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I want to thank you for your assistance today. We've come to the end of questions for you. It has been of assistance to us, and we thank you for being available there in Belgrade. We need to close down the television link that we now have, so you are now of course free to go back to your normal activities. Once more, we thank you and the Court staff in Belgrade for the assistance today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If there is no other matter, we need now to adjourn, to resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 19th day of May, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.49 p.m.,
